extraction.body: Do AI coding tools actually make developers more productive? It depends on how you define productivity. After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped. The researchers found that synchronous agents (agents that write and edit code with the developer in real time) produced a 741% increase in lines of code and led to a 65% increase in pull requests. However, software releases only rose 20%. Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types. The researchers concluded that the productivity of AI tools is weakened at later stages of software development due to “human bottlenecks.” What’s the holdup? IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools. While coding tools can accelerate code generation, Jennings said, they often don’t contribute to testing, validations, reviews, and other stages of the software development life cycle that still require human oversight and ultimately hold up production. “What AI coding has done is it compressed the ability to write code, so now we can write code much faster, but just because you can write code much faster doesn’t mean that you can actually do a lot of the other steps faster,” Jennings said. From cybersecurity and big data to cloud computing, IT Brew covers the latest trends shaping business tech in our 4x weekly newsletter, virtual events with industry experts, and digital guides. Sounds familiar? This isn’t the first time researchers have undermined the productivity gains of AI tools. A recent GitLab report, which surveyed 1,528 DevSecOps pros, also found that 85% believe AI has “shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it.” “Compliance, security scanning, deployment, and incident response are where AI velocity stops and the rest of the life cycle waits,” the report wrote. IT Brew also previously reported on a research study from AI research nonprofit METR, which found some developers took 19% more time to complete assigned tasks when using AI coding tools. Jennings said the study’s findings should be an eye-opener for tech leaders, who should readjust their expectations of how AI coding tools contribute to their bottom line moving forward. “Delivered code is not delivered value, it’s something that’s going to help us deliver more value, but now we have to pay more attention to the other steps in the process,” he said. sources.title: Dan Adler Warns AI Coding Agents Are Flooding Legacy Codebases With Code No One Understands - BigGo Finance
passages: It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends.
The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.
Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems.
Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code.
They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding.
Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist.
Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving.

The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required.
Adler's argument is counterintuitive: the AI tools that are making developers dramatically more productive are simultaneously undermining the stability of the codebases that run the world.
He calls it "a tsunami of code" — code being generated faster than enterprises can review, understand, or integrate it.

He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising.
By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code.
Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk.
The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says.

The second unnamed quote Adler surfaces comes from a technical leader at a top-ten US bank, described as holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets in custody or under management: "Of course Claude Code can make this change, but I need to do it in 90,000 repositories." The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm.

Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge?

sources.title: AI coding agents need good software engineers
passages: Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed.
You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it.
This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous.

As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code.
You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo.
In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer.
In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline.
That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?
It’s important to realize that generating code has never been the hard part of software.

extraction.body: For the past year, Silicon Valley has been telling us that software development is on the verge of becoming a prompt-and-ship exercise. You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it. Sure, maybe you could keep a few token senior engineers around to bless the output…or maybe not. I mean, Google’s Sundar Pichai says 75% of its new code is now AI-generated and reviewed by engineers, up sharply from earlier levels. Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed. When people who helped build the tools used by millions start warning that those same tools can produce buggy, potentially dangerous software at industrial scale, it’s probably time to rethink some of the assumptions fueling the AI wave. The right answer isn’t “AI coding is bad.” That’s silly. AI coding is powerful in roughly the same way power tools are powerful. Nearly correct is still very wrong I've made a related argument about the real cost of “nearly correct” AI code. It’s important to realize that generating code has never been the hard part of software. As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code. AI hasn’t eliminated the need for that hard work. But a final draft that’s only 80% right is a liability, so I have to coach and oversee the agents. The problem is abdication The dumbest version of the AI coding debate asks whether AI will replace developers. Instead, it rewards the person who can tell, quickly and accurately, whether the output fits the system, the security model, the performance envelope, the user need, and the organization’s standards. In other words, AI rewards experience; it rewards people who know what “good” looks like. This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous. Not because agents can’t be useful, but because responsibility doesn’t scale the way prompts do. But when a company starts celebrating dozens or hundreds of agents churning out pull requests, issues, tests, migrations, and fixes, the obvious question is: Who actually understands what’s happening? If the answer is “another agent,” I’m sorry but we’re back where we started. InfoWorld reported that GitHub has considered stronger filters and maintainer controls to stem the flood. It’s cheap to generate but expensive to review. In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer. This is why the “human in the loop” language, tired as it has become, still matters. A junior developer accepting generated code because it passes the first test doesn’t solve the problem. Nor does a senior developer “reviewing” a flood of agent-written pull requests at a speed that makes real review impossible. For developers, AI is strongest when it’s used for bounded tasks like generating tests or explaining unfamiliar code. For managers, the worst possible metric is “percentage of code generated by AI.” That’s like measuring a newsroom by the percentage of sentences drafted by autocomplete. The 2025 DORA report on the state of AI-assisted software development gets at this more usefully: AI tends to amplify an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses. If you have strong tests, clear ownership, disciplined review, good observability, and fast rollback, AI can make you better. In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline. You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo. At scale, keeping a human in the loop has to be enforced by architecture, not good intentions. In practice this means baking guardrails into the systems agents touch, like identity, data governance, and observability. The genuinely interesting shift I see across the industry, and yes, where Oracle is placing its bet, is pushing more of those controls down into the data layer itself, so agents operate against governed enterprise data rather than as clever scripts holding the keys to production. That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?

But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff.

These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code .
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.

After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.

Manav Khurana, GitLab’s chief product and marketing officer, added it’s important for organizations using AI coding tools to invest in agentic infrastructure to support other steps of the software development life cycle: “If they don’t have the right agentic infrastructure to make sure that code created can become shipped software with the right level of automation, they also risk that the new code creates reliability problems, or security problems, or cost overruns, because speed sometimes also brings with it chaos.”
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.

extraction.body: Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.” Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026. To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write. In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms. While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work. AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.
Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems.
Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code.
They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding.
Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist.
Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving.

The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required.
Adler's argument is counterintuitive: the AI tools that are making developers dramatically more productive are simultaneously undermining the stability of the codebases that run the world.
He calls it "a tsunami of code" — code being generated faster than enterprises can review, understand, or integrate it.

He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising.
By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code.
Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk.
The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says.

The second unnamed quote Adler surfaces comes from a technical leader at a top-ten US bank, described as holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets in custody or under management: "Of course Claude Code can make this change, but I need to do it in 90,000 repositories." The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm.

Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge?

extraction.body: One of the most senior technical leaders at a top-ten automaker said something recently that should stop anyone who thinks AI coding tools are a solved problem: "I don't know what this code does. AI wrote it for me." The context was autopilot code, with thousands of engineers to manage and resource. Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems. Adler's argument is counterintuitive: the AI tools that are making developers dramatically more productive are simultaneously undermining the stability of the codebases that run the world. He calls it "a tsunami of code" — code being generated faster than enterprises can review, understand, or integrate it. Adler opens with a demographic point that reframes where software actually lives. By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code. The public image of software as a startup-and-solo-founder industry, he argues, describes almost none of the real workforce. The systems these engineers maintain are unglamorous but critical: real-time transaction rejection at a bank, reimbursement-rate calculation for a dual-coverage insurance policyholder, warehouse scanning behind Amazon deliveries, Uber arrival estimates, radar-based flight-path adjustment, payroll issuance, office air conditioning running continuously. "The software that runs the world is not attractive. It is not new. It is not clean. This is how everything really works," Adler said. He frames the session explicitly as "a call to honor the people, the owners of these codebases" — the maintainers doing what he describes as "the thankless but fundamental work." The core tension Adler identifies is between generation speed and comprehension capacity. Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving. But the codebases receiving this output are too large to review efficiently. He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising. The root cause is scale. Millions of lines of code across tens of thousands of repositories cannot fit in a context window or even be cloned and processed in real time. Adler calls this "simply impossible." Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code. They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding. His claim is that repository architecture documented in agents.md files "changes almost nothing" in practice. The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says. But there is a hard limit: "You can't search for something you literally can't see." Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist. He names the vendors he claims are not solving this: OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, and "anyone else." His concession is that their agents are "so incredibly good at solving the small tasks that most developers face every day" that demand is growing faster than ever — which is precisely why the large-scale breakdown goes unnoticed. The second unnamed quote Adler surfaces comes from a technical leader at a top-ten US bank, described as holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets in custody or under management: "Of course Claude Code can make this change, but I need to do it in 90,000 repositories." The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm. The point: when agents discover and create vulnerabilities at unprecedented rates, telling a bank to use a coding agent to fix them doesn't address the problem of mapping how 90,000 repositories interact across all products. Adler's prescription is a fundamental graph of the codebase — including search and accurate compiler output — sitting in front of the agent. His formulation: "Visibility is infrastructure." The claim is that if you conduct this analysis, you empower agents to make changes effectively across the whole system rather than within a single repository. He predicts the code volume only grows: "These huge code bases are not going anywhere. In fact, there will be even more code." The question Adler does not fully answer is whether this visibility layer becomes a durable independent infrastructure business or simply a feature that frontier labs eventually fold into their own products. He acknowledges that model quality keeps improving and that major vendors will eventually add such capabilities. The tension sits unresolved. Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk. The product is designed to let an owner of a massive codebase commit changes to hundreds or thousands of repositories simultaneously from a single prompt. The design principle is a split between agentic and deterministic execution: The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required. Adler emphasizes the tracking and auditing capability: confirming 100% coverage of locations needing a patch or change. The one customer proof point Adler offered comes from an early-access user at Merkari, which he describes as a global trading service from Japan with hundreds of independent microservices in production. The user was fixing a code injection issue on GitHub involving environment variables. He ran the product on two repositories where he already knew the problem existed, then let the agent explore the rest of the codebase. It found 80 more potential vulnerabilities — all in configuration files. Adler frames this as scanning and fixing in one pass via a deterministic script that guarantees consistent changes across hundreds of locations. "This is where confidence lies in the age of agent programming," he said. The unresolved question is whether this audit-and-coverage guarantee holds up at the 90,000-repository scale Adler cites as the bank's requirement. The only published proof point is a two-repository seed expanding to 80 findings. Adler's most striking framing deserves mention on its own terms: "The threat comes from within. The same tools that speed up our work and allow us to write more code faster than ever before are also creating the conditions under which these vast codebases that run our world are starting to break down." This is not an anti-AI argument. It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends. The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review. Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge? For the software industry, the stakes are concentrated: the same companies driving AI adoption — large enterprises with thousands of repositories — are the ones least equipped to absorb the output. Whether Sourcegraph's visibility infrastructure, or an equivalent from another vendor, becomes the standard layer for managing AI-generated code at scale will determine whether the productivity gains from AI coding tools translate into durable software quality, or into a maintenance burden that compounds with every passing day.

sources.title: AI coding agents need good software engineers
passages: Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed.
You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it.
This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous.

As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code.
You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo.

extraction.body: For the past year, Silicon Valley has been telling us that software development is on the verge of becoming a prompt-and-ship exercise. You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it. Sure, maybe you could keep a few token senior engineers around to bless the output…or maybe not. I mean, Google’s Sundar Pichai says 75% of its new code is now AI-generated and reviewed by engineers, up sharply from earlier levels. Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed. When people who helped build the tools used by millions start warning that those same tools can produce buggy, potentially dangerous software at industrial scale, it’s probably time to rethink some of the assumptions fueling the AI wave. The right answer isn’t “AI coding is bad.” That’s silly. AI coding is powerful in roughly the same way power tools are powerful. Nearly correct is still very wrong I've made a related argument about the real cost of “nearly correct” AI code. It’s important to realize that generating code has never been the hard part of software. As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code. AI hasn’t eliminated the need for that hard work. But a final draft that’s only 80% right is a liability, so I have to coach and oversee the agents. The problem is abdication The dumbest version of the AI coding debate asks whether AI will replace developers. Instead, it rewards the person who can tell, quickly and accurately, whether the output fits the system, the security model, the performance envelope, the user need, and the organization’s standards. In other words, AI rewards experience; it rewards people who know what “good” looks like. This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous. Not because agents can’t be useful, but because responsibility doesn’t scale the way prompts do. But when a company starts celebrating dozens or hundreds of agents churning out pull requests, issues, tests, migrations, and fixes, the obvious question is: Who actually understands what’s happening? If the answer is “another agent,” I’m sorry but we’re back where we started. InfoWorld reported that GitHub has considered stronger filters and maintainer controls to stem the flood. It’s cheap to generate but expensive to review. In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer. This is why the “human in the loop” language, tired as it has become, still matters. A junior developer accepting generated code because it passes the first test doesn’t solve the problem. Nor does a senior developer “reviewing” a flood of agent-written pull requests at a speed that makes real review impossible. For developers, AI is strongest when it’s used for bounded tasks like generating tests or explaining unfamiliar code. For managers, the worst possible metric is “percentage of code generated by AI.” That’s like measuring a newsroom by the percentage of sentences drafted by autocomplete. The 2025 DORA report on the state of AI-assisted software development gets at this more usefully: AI tends to amplify an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses. If you have strong tests, clear ownership, disciplined review, good observability, and fast rollback, AI can make you better. In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline. You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo. At scale, keeping a human in the loop has to be enforced by architecture, not good intentions. In practice this means baking guardrails into the systems agents touch, like identity, data governance, and observability. The genuinely interesting shift I see across the industry, and yes, where Oracle is placing its bet, is pushing more of those controls down into the data layer itself, so agents operate against governed enterprise data rather than as clever scripts holding the keys to production. That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?

sources.title: Cloudflare acquires Deno to improve its Workers programming model
passages: According to Cloudflare’s Kenton Varda, Cloudflare will use this acquisition to improve its Workers programming model and platform, which allows customers to build and run software on Cloudflare’s network. (Varda is principal engineer for Cloudflare Workers.)
Deno — which was co-founded by Bert Belder and Node.js creator Ryan Dahl — recently launched celld, an open source implementation of Workers, which Varda wrote “delighted” the Cloudflare team.

Varda argued that contrary to “a popular theory” that the company “made Cloudflare Workers work differently from other cloud platforms in order to create ‘lock-in,’” the company believes “being open source and giving people an escape hatch is good business .”
Cloudflare announced Friday that it’s acquiring Deno, the startup behind the programming runtime of the same name.
The financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.
Deno had raised a total of $26 million , including a Series A led by Sequoia.

passages: Cloudflare has announced the acquisition of startup Deno, which develops the eponymous code runtime.
The company plans to use the deal to advance the programming model and the Cloudflare Workers platform, which enables customers to build and run software on Cloudflare’s network, TechCrunch reports .
Deno was founded by Bert Belder and Node.js creator Ryan Dahl.
Dahl said his team is joining Cloudflare to turn the Workers programming model into a widespread way of developing servers.
He also noted that the Cloudflare team welcomed Deno’s launch of the celld project—an open implementation of Workers.
He contrasted this position with the widespread assumption, he said, that Cloudflare made Workers different from other cloud platforms in order to lock customers into its service.
The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
According to TechCrunch, Deno has raised a total of $26 million in investment, including in a Series A round led by Sequoia.

sources.title: Cloudflare Absorbs Entire Deno Development Team, Consolidating Workers for Self-Hosted Operations - BigGo Finance
passages: U.S. cloud computing giant Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire team behind "Deno," the JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, will join the company.

The Deno development team, led by Ryan Dahl—the creator of Node.js—will embark on integration work to enable Cloudflare's serverless platform "Workers" to run in full production on self-managed infrastructure.

Dahl proved with Node.js that "you can write servers in JavaScript," refined that design with Deno, and is now aiming to make the Workers programming model—a distributed execution paradigm with compute, database, queues, and real-time communication built in—the mainstream approach for self-hosted operations.
At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud.
In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform.
Deno's decision to come under Cloudflare's umbrella follows a pricing skirmish that surfaced over the past two months.
When Deno unveiled celld in August, it offered a pricing structure significantly cheaper than Cloudflare Workers, initiating a price competition.
Paid Deno Deploy customers will receive migration assistance to Cloudflare Workers, but no specific support measures for free-tier users have been announced.

Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services.
In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in.

extraction.body: U.S. cloud computing giant Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire team behind "Deno," the JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, will join the company. The Deno development team, led by Ryan Dahl—the creator of Node.js—will embark on integration work to enable Cloudflare's serverless platform "Workers" to run in full production on self-managed infrastructure. The announcement was posted on Cloudflare's official blog under the joint bylines of Dahl and the company's Kenton Varda. Deno published the same announcement on its own blog the same day. Neither company disclosed transaction terms, including any acquisition price. At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud. In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform. Going forward, the team will integrate celld with "workerd," the Workers runtime that Cloudflare has open-sourced, evolving it into a formally supported self-hosted solution. Dahl and Bert Belder will lead this effort. Dahl stated, "I'm joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model the mainstream way to build servers." Deno's leadership has decided to concentrate development resources on this shared foundation rather than continuing to operate an independent runtime and hosting service. With the integration, a phased wind-down plan has been outlined for Deno's existing products and services. Note: Timeline based on official announcements from both companies. Deno is a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime that Dahl unveiled in 2018, designed to address architectural shortcomings in Node.js with a more secure and modern approach. Dahl led Node.js's early development before leaving the project in 2012. In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in. His argument is straightforward: workerd is open source, and the code published is identical to what runs in Cloudflare's production environment. He noted there are actual cases of users migrating away from Workers using it. "Open-sourcing and providing an escape hatch is actually good business," Varda argued. He then identified the real challenge: workerd's Durable Objects only support a single instance and cannot scale. celld fills this gap, and it will be the core focus of the Deno team's work after joining. Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services. The answer that emerged was celld, a single binary written in Rust. celld's only external dependency is a single object storage bucket. It bakes all the fundamental elements of distributed processing—compute, relational database, queues, and WebSockets—directly into the programming model. sources.title: Cloudflare Absorbs Entire Deno Development Team, Consolidating Workers for Self-Hosted Operations - BigGo Finance
passages: U.S. cloud computing giant Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire team behind "Deno," the JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, will join the company.

The Deno development team, led by Ryan Dahl—the creator of Node.js—will embark on integration work to enable Cloudflare's serverless platform "Workers" to run in full production on self-managed infrastructure.

Dahl proved with Node.js that "you can write servers in JavaScript," refined that design with Deno, and is now aiming to make the Workers programming model—a distributed execution paradigm with compute, database, queues, and real-time communication built in—the mainstream approach for self-hosted operations.
At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud.
In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform.
Deno's decision to come under Cloudflare's umbrella follows a pricing skirmish that surfaced over the past two months.
When Deno unveiled celld in August, it offered a pricing structure significantly cheaper than Cloudflare Workers, initiating a price competition.
Paid Deno Deploy customers will receive migration assistance to Cloudflare Workers, but no specific support measures for free-tier users have been announced.

Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services.
In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in.

extraction.body: U.S. cloud computing giant Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire team behind "Deno," the JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, will join the company. The Deno development team, led by Ryan Dahl—the creator of Node.js—will embark on integration work to enable Cloudflare's serverless platform "Workers" to run in full production on self-managed infrastructure. The announcement was posted on Cloudflare's official blog under the joint bylines of Dahl and the company's Kenton Varda. Deno published the same announcement on its own blog the same day. Neither company disclosed transaction terms, including any acquisition price. At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud. In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform. Going forward, the team will integrate celld with "workerd," the Workers runtime that Cloudflare has open-sourced, evolving it into a formally supported self-hosted solution. Dahl and Bert Belder will lead this effort. Dahl stated, "I'm joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model the mainstream way to build servers." Deno's leadership has decided to concentrate development resources on this shared foundation rather than continuing to operate an independent runtime and hosting service. With the integration, a phased wind-down plan has been outlined for Deno's existing products and services. Note: Timeline based on official announcements from both companies. Deno is a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime that Dahl unveiled in 2018, designed to address architectural shortcomings in Node.js with a more secure and modern approach. Dahl led Node.js's early development before leaving the project in 2012. In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in. His argument is straightforward: workerd is open source, and the code published is identical to what runs in Cloudflare's production environment. He noted there are actual cases of users migrating away from Workers using it. "Open-sourcing and providing an escape hatch is actually good business," Varda argued. He then identified the real challenge: workerd's Durable Objects only support a single instance and cannot scale. celld fills this gap, and it will be the core focus of the Deno team's work after joining. Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services. The answer that emerged was celld, a single binary written in Rust. celld's only external dependency is a single object storage bucket. It bakes all the fundamental elements of distributed processing—compute, relational database, queues, and WebSockets—directly into the programming model. In Dahl's words, "Scalability should be built into the programming model; each application shouldn't have to assemble its own infrastructure." The reason celld chose Cloudflare Workers' programming model as its foundation is the Durable Objects abstraction. Each Durable Object functions as a small, individually addressable server with an embedded SQLite database, runs single-threaded, and comes standard with synchronous access to a local database and WebSockets. Dahl sees this type of abstraction as particularly useful for agent harnesses—the execution substrate for AI agents—because it combines serverless execution, persistent state, WebSockets, and a high-level JavaScript interface all in one. Deno's decision to come under Cloudflare's umbrella follows a pricing skirmish that surfaced over the past two months. When Deno unveiled celld in August, it offered a pricing structure significantly cheaper than Cloudflare Workers, initiating a price competition. Cloudflare pushed back, creating tension between the two parties. Additionally, late last year, Oven—the company behind the JavaScript runtime "Bun"—was acquired by AI company Anthropic, a similar development in the same space. The pattern of independent runtime developers being absorbed into larger platform companies continues. However, there are important differences between the Bun acquisition and Deno's integration. In Bun's case, Anthropic was seen as leveraging the runtime technology itself to strengthen its own AI infrastructure. In Deno's case, the primary focus is expanding the ecosystem of Cloudflare's existing Workers product. It is less an acquisition and more an integration of projects heading in the same direction. This announcement marks a major turning point for developers who have built applications on Deno. With official development of the Deno runtime ending after a one-year grace period, existing users will need to consider migration options. Paid Deno Deploy customers will receive migration assistance to Cloudflare Workers, but no specific support measures for free-tier users have been announced. On the other hand, Deno's survival as an open-source project is guaranteed, leaving the door open for the community to fork and continue development. JSR will also continue operating, meaning part of the Deno ecosystem will live on atop Cloudflare's infrastructure. The JavaScript server-side world has seen multiple runtimes compete since Node.js debuted in 2009. Dahl proved with Node.js that "you can write servers in JavaScript," refined that design with Deno, and is now aiming to make the Workers programming model—a distributed execution paradigm with compute, database, queues, and real-time communication built in—the mainstream approach for self-hosted operations. The loss of yet another independent runtime option is a short-term blow for developers, but for the broader JavaScript server ecosystem, it may serve as a catalyst for wider adoption of a programming model that hides the complexity of distributed systems. passages: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died.
In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.
And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.
Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959.
Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article.
In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said. She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.” “She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.” Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.

But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.”

Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said.
She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.”
“She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.”
Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

sources.title: Margaret Hamilton, pioneering Apollo program software engineer, dies at 90
passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics told MIT News."Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers.

The trailblazing pioneer played a crucial role in the development of flight software for NASA's Apollo Program, which was responsible for taking humans to the moon for the first time. Hamilton was an integral part of NASA's Apollo program, which landed human beings on the moon for the first time in 1969.

Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon." She also was granted the NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for her scientific and technical contributions.Hamilton has connections throughout the Midwest.

Hamilton was given the medal by President Barack Obama in 2016. Obama said at the time, "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history.

sources.title: Margaret Hamilton, pioneering Apollo program software engineer, dies at 90
passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible.

“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university’s communications office.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.

“She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.”

Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT’s Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said.
She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.”
“She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.”
Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

extraction.body: TULSA, Okla. — The BOK Center announced country music singer Ella Langley's Friday night concert has been canceled due to a "serious security threat." The BOK Center released a statement that said in part, "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first." FOX23 reached out to the Tulsa Police Department who said they believe the threat was likely a swatting call. According to TPD, officers carried out their regular security check they conduct before each concert and found nothing of concern. On Friday morning, authorities said they received a phone call threatening harm at the concert, though they said no details were specified by the caller. Following the call, the department said they conducted another security sweep of the venue and upped its security personnel at the BOK Center. TPD said they found no credible threat and believe there is no active threat at this time. The department said they did not advise either the BOK Center or Langley to cancel the concert, stating the decision to cancel the show was likely made either by the BOK Center itself or Langley's team. The BOK Center said information about ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. You can view the BOK Center's full statement below: The Tulsa Police Department released the following written and verbal statement addressing the situation: A sold-out concert was canceled tonight over threats of violence. Before the event, we swept the area with our K-9, Bomb Team, Patrol and BOK security for anything dangerous. Out of an abundance of caution, we swept the building and surrounding area and again found no credible threat to the event's safety. We advised the performer's staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway. If you know anything about it that can be helpful and want a cash reward, call Tulsa Crime Stoppers at 918-596-COPS. Langley released the following statement on her social media: "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue and my security team.

The BOK Center released a statement that said in part, "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.
According to TPD, officers carried out their regular security check they conduct before each concert and found nothing of concern.
On Friday morning, authorities said they received a phone call threatening harm at the concert, though they said no details were specified by the caller.
We advised the performer's staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway.

Ella Langley won't be taking the stage in Oklahoma tonight ... her show's been canceled due to a "serious security threat." Tulsa's BOK Center took to social media to announce the abrupt cancellation, writing ...

update 4:12 PM PT -- Tulsa Police Department posted a statement on Facebook, saying they found "no credible threat" after "a call was made threatening the lives of people attending the event." Police say the caller threatened to do "great harm" to concertgoers, through "shots fired and bombs." They said they did a sweep with their bomb dogs after the call and didn't find anything.
They say neither the police nor the BOK Center pulled the plug ... explaining it was Ella's team who decided to back out.

“Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show,” Langley, 27, captioned the post on Instagram.
“This is not a decision that was made lightly.
Tulsa Police said that the agency “advised the performer’s staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway.”

The BOK Center released a statement that said in part, "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first." FOX23 reached out to the Tulsa Police Department who said they believe the threat was likely a swatting call. According to TPD, officers carried out their regular security check they conduct before each concert and found nothing of concern. On Friday morning, authorities said they received a phone call threatening harm at the concert, though they said no details were specified by the caller. Following the call, the department said they conducted another security sweep of the venue and upped its security personnel at the BOK Center. TPD said they found no credible threat and believe there is no active threat at this time. The department said they did not advise either the BOK Center or Langley to cancel the concert, stating the decision to cancel the show was likely made either by the BOK Center itself or Langley's team. The BOK Center said information about ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. You can view the BOK Center's full statement below: The Tulsa Police Department released the following written and verbal statement addressing the situation: A sold-out concert was canceled tonight over threats of violence. Before the event, we swept the area with our K-9, Bomb Team, Patrol and BOK security for anything dangerous. Out of an abundance of caution, we swept the building and surrounding area and again found no credible threat to the event's safety. We advised the performer's staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway. If you know anything about it that can be helpful and want a cash reward, call Tulsa Crime Stoppers at 918-596-COPS. Langley released the following statement on her social media: "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue and my security team.

extraction.body: TypeSafe AI, the developer of Jev, a new type of AI model that gained rapid popularity after launching just a few weeks ago, has raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Sequoia and existing investor DCVC. The massive fundraise comes as little surprise given Jev went viral almost instantly after its September 15 release . The startup claims that a third of Fortune 500 companies are already using the model, a remarkably swift adoption by enterprises. Jev is based on a transformer architecture, but it is not a large language model (LLM). extraction.body: TypeSafe AI just closed an $870 million funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz, valuing the startup at $7.5 billion just weeks after launching its groundbreaking non-text AI model Jev. The staggering valuation puts TypeSafe among the most valuable AI startups globally, signaling massive investor appetite for alternatives to traditional language models. TypeSafe AI just pulled off one of the year's most dramatic funding rounds, raising $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation mere weeks after unveiling Jev, its revolutionary non-text AI model. While most AI companies spend months or years proving their technology before commanding billion-dollar valuations, TypeSafe's Jev model appears to have struck an immediate chord with investors. The non-text approach represents a fundamental departure from the language model arms race that's dominated AI funding, potentially opening entirely new categories of machine intelligence. [Embedded image: TypeSafe AI team celebrating funding announcement] The $7.5 billion valuation puts TypeSafe in rarified air. For context, Cognition recently hit a $48 billion valuation in the AI coding space, while other specialized AI startups have struggled to break the billion-dollar barrier. The speed of TypeSafe's ascent suggests Jev addresses a critical gap in current AI capabilities. What makes Jev different isn't just its non-text focus - it's the potential applications. While traditional large language models excel at text generation and analysis, they hit walls when dealing with other data types. The funding landscape for AI infrastructure has been brutal lately. Rising bond yields have hammered AI infrastructure funding, making debt-heavy data center buildouts prohibitively expensive. But TypeSafe's equity raise suggests investors see Jev as fundamentally different - a software breakthrough rather than a capital-intensive infrastructure play. The firm's bet on TypeSafe signals confidence that non-text AI represents the next major platform shift, potentially as significant as the move from rule-based systems to neural networks. OpenAI's recent DevDay showcased new Dots agents, but those still rely fundamentally on language model architectures. If Jev proves superior for non-text tasks, it could force a wholesale rethinking of AI development strategies across the industry. The secrecy around Jev's technical details mirrors the broader trend of world model AI startups going dark despite massive funding. But TypeSafe's willingness to launch publicly, even with limited technical disclosure, suggests confidence in their competitive moat. Most companies have barely begun integrating text-based AI into their workflows. If non-text models like Jev prove more versatile for real-world applications - think manufacturing sensors, medical imaging, or autonomous systems - it could leapfrog the current generation of AI deployments entirely. The $870 million war chest gives TypeSafe serious runway to prove Jev's capabilities at scale. Unlike hardware-intensive AI companies that burn through funding on GPU clusters, software-focused approaches like TypeSafe's can stretch capital further while iterating rapidly on core algorithms. TypeSafe's meteoric rise from launch to $7.5 billion valuation in weeks represents more than just another AI funding milestone - it signals a potential paradigm shift toward specialized, non-text AI architectures. With Andreessen Horowitz's backing and $870 million in fresh capital, the company now faces the challenge of proving that Jev can deliver on its revolutionary promise. For an industry still grappling with the limits of language models, TypeSafe's success or failure could determine whether the next wave of AI breakthroughs comes from scaling existing approaches or fundamentally reimagining how machines process information.
