sources.title: One Year After the Crash: Bitcoin and Ethereum Order Book Depth Recovers, Altcoins Continue to Lose Liquidity - KuCoin
passages: DeepOcean Summary: After comparing order book depth on centralized exchanges at four time points, CoinDesk Research found that the USD depth for Bitcoin and Ethereum is now higher than during the crash and at the beginning of 2025 and 2026, indicating genuine position accumulation by market makers.
For those still treating the “altcoin season” as the default path for liquidity rotation, this marks a structural turning point one year later.
“A year ago, we wrote that liquidity was thin and fragmented, and it was unclear where capital would rotate once the dust settled.
“Market makers have returned to major cryptocurrencies, with liquidity now exceeding pre-crash levels, while altcoin liquidity as a whole continues to decline.
Beyond a select few altcoins, I expect this divergence to persist into next year, as major cryptocurrencies will continue to dominate institutional interest and trading volume.”
One year after the largest forced liquidation event in crypto history, market "pipelines" show divergent narratives.
On October 7, there were approximately $11.7 million in orders within a 1% price range.
The rebuilt order book underwent an initial test earlier this week.
As the market sold off, Bitcoin’s 1% depth decreased by approximately 12% between October 7 and October 8.
The tightest spread bands for Ethereum slightly widened, while orders further away from the price increased.
Depth refers to the value of buy and sell orders near the current price.
The deeper the order book, the larger the volume of large trades that can be absorbed without significantly moving the price.
Several days after reaching a historic high of over $126,000, Bitcoin dropped to around $122,600 during early trading on October 10, 2025.

Hours later, it fell below $105,000, with a significant portion of the decline occurring during thin trading hours on Friday evening in the U.S., when President Donald Trump announced a 100% tariff on Chinese imported goods.
Over $19 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated in a single day.
Measured by token volume, altcoin depth appears healthier: it peaked on January 1 of this year and has since declined only modestly.
Altcoin liquidity, on the other hand, has moved in the opposite direction: USD depth has steadily declined since early 2025, a trend masked by falling token prices.

Meanwhile, USD depth for altcoins has weakened continuously since early 2025, with weekly spot trading volumes still about two-thirds lower than during the crash week. For those still treating the “altcoin season” as the default path for liquidity rotation, this marks a structural turning point one year later. The order books for Bitcoin and Ethereum are deeper than before the crash, while altcoin liquidity continues to drain, and spot trading volumes remain far below the peak seen in October 2025. The order books for Bitcoin and Ethereum are deeper than they were on the day of the crash and at the beginning of 2025 and 2026, and the increase in USD terms reflects market makers deploying more capital, not just lower coin prices. Altcoin liquidity, on the other hand, has moved in the opposite direction: USD depth has steadily declined since early 2025, a trend masked by falling token prices. Weekly spot trading volume has declined by nearly two-thirds compared to the week of the crash, despite roughly doubling from the August low. One year after the largest forced liquidation event in crypto history, market "pipelines" show divergent narratives. Order book liquidity for Bitcoin and Ethereum is now higher than on the day of the crash or at the beginning of this year; smaller-cap tokens and spot trading have not followed suit. Several days after reaching a historic high of over $126,000, Bitcoin dropped to around $122,600 during early trading on October 10, 2025. Hours later, it fell below $105,000, with a significant portion of the decline occurring during thin trading hours on Friday evening in the U.S., when President Donald Trump announced a 100% tariff on Chinese imported goods. Over $19 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated in a single day. To measure the subsequent recovery, CoinDesk Research compared the market depth of major centralized exchanges at four points in time: January 1, 2025; October 10, 2025; January 1, 2026; and this week. Depth refers to the value of buy and sell orders near the current price. The deeper the order book, the larger the volume of large trades that can be absorbed without significantly moving the price. The order book for Bitcoin is now deeper than at any previous point mentioned. On October 7, there were approximately $11.7 million in orders within a 1% price range. This represents about a 75% increase compared to the crash day a year ago, and is higher than the approximately $9 million at the beginning of this year and the roughly $6.9 million at the start of 2025. This is not a price effect. Bitcoin is currently trading at about two-thirds of its pre-crash price, so the deeper order book in dollar terms reflects market makers committing more capital, not just coins becoming cheaper. Improvements are concentrated near the price—the range where market makers are most active. Further out, at a 5% distance from the price, depth is approximately $24 million, roughly returning to levels seen in January 2025. Ethereum's recovery has been stronger in some respects. Depth within a 0.5% price range has more than doubled since the crash day, reaching approximately $4.2 million. At the 1% level, depth has risen by about three-quarters to approximately $5.3 million, surpassing both January readings. "The deepening of major cryptocurrencies represents real capital, not a price effect," said CoinDesk researcher Saksham Diwan. The rebuilt order book underwent an initial test earlier this week. As the market sold off, Bitcoin’s 1% depth decreased by approximately 12% between October 7 and October 8. The tightest spread bands for Ethereum slightly widened, while orders further away from the price increased. For altcoins, the picture is exactly the opposite. In CoinDesk Research’s altcoin basket, USD depth was highest on January 1, 2025, and has been lower at every subsequent measurement point. Depth at 5% from the price has declined by about one-third since early 2025, to approximately $2 million. At the closer 1% level, it has decreased by about one-sixth. Measured by token volume, altcoin depth appears healthier: it peaked on January 1 of this year and has since declined only modestly. However, analysts note that the "recovery" in token units has been primarily driven by price declines, masking the ongoing erosion of committed capital. Spot trading has not yet resumed. According to CoinDesk Research, the average weekly spot trading volume on centralized exchanges over the four weeks ending September 27 was approximately $279 billion, nearly two-thirds lower than the $801 billion recorded during the crash week. Activity hit its lowest point in August, when weekly trading volume dropped to around $135 billion, and has since doubled. However, it remains far below levels seen before and after the crash. On October 10, 2025, crypto liquidity evaporated within hours. Where it would go next was an open question. “A year ago, we wrote that liquidity was thin and fragmented, and it was unclear where capital would rotate once the dust settled. Now we have the answer: Bitcoin and Ethereum,” said Joshua de Vos, Head of Research at CoinDesk. “Market makers have returned to major cryptocurrencies, with liquidity now exceeding pre-crash levels, while altcoin liquidity as a whole continues to decline. Beyond a select few altcoins, I expect this divergence to persist into next year, as major cryptocurrencies will continue to dominate institutional interest and trading volume.”

coreStoryFacts.text: DeepOcean Summary: After comparing order book depth on centralized exchanges at four time points, CoinDesk Research found that the USD depth for Bitcoin and Ethereum is now higher than during the crash and at the beginning of 2025 and 2026, indicating genuine position accumulation by market makers.
For those still treating the “altcoin season” as the default path for liquidity rotation, this marks a structural turning point one year later.
“A year ago, we wrote that liquidity was thin and fragmented, and it was unclear where capital would rotate once the dust settled.
“Market makers have returned to major cryptocurrencies, with liquidity now exceeding pre-crash levels, while altcoin liquidity as a whole continues to decline.
Beyond a select few altcoins, I expect this divergence to persist into next year, as major cryptocurrencies will continue to dominate institutional interest and trading volume.”
One year after the largest forced liquidation event in crypto history, market "pipelines" show divergent narratives.
On October 7, there were approximately $11.7 million in orders within a 1% price range.
The rebuilt order book underwent an initial test earlier this week.
As the market sold off, Bitcoin’s 1% depth decreased by approximately 12% between October 7 and October 8.
The tightest spread bands for Ethereum slightly widened, while orders further away from the price increased.
Depth refers to the value of buy and sell orders near the current price.
The deeper the order book, the larger the volume of large trades that can be absorbed without significantly moving the price.
Several days after reaching a historic high of over $126,000, Bitcoin dropped to around $122,600 during early trading on October 10, 2025.

Hours later, it fell below $105,000, with a significant portion of the decline occurring during thin trading hours on Friday evening in the U.S., when President Donald Trump announced a 100% tariff on Chinese imported goods.
Over $19 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated in a single day.
Measured by token volume, altcoin depth appears healthier: it peaked on January 1 of this year and has since declined only modestly.
Altcoin liquidity, on the other hand, has moved in the opposite direction: USD depth has steadily declined since early 2025, a trend masked by falling token prices.
“ A year ago , we wrote that liquidity was thin and fragmented, and that it was unclear where capital would rotate once the dust settled.
We now have an answer: bitcoin and ether,” said Joshua de Vos, Research lead at CoinDesk.
“Market makers have returned to majors, with liquidity above pre-crash levels, whilst altcoin liquidity continues to trend down as a whole.
Beyond a select few alts, I expect this divergence to persist into next year as majors continue to dominate institutional interest and volumes.”

Smaller tokens and spot trading, however, have not followed.
Bitcoin’s order book is deeper now than on any of those earlier dates.

passages: DeepOcean Summary: After comparing order book depth on centralized exchanges at four time points, CoinDesk Research found that the USD depth for Bitcoin and Ethereum is now higher than during the crash and at the beginning of 2025 and 2026, indicating genuine position accumulation by market makers.
For those still treating the “altcoin season” as the default path for liquidity rotation, this marks a structural turning point one year later.
“A year ago, we wrote that liquidity was thin and fragmented, and it was unclear where capital would rotate once the dust settled.

One year after the largest forced liquidation event in crypto history, market "pipelines" show divergent narratives.
On October 7, there were approximately $11.7 million in orders within a 1% price range.

The deeper the order book, the larger the volume of large trades that can be absorbed without significantly moving the price.

extraction.body: DeepOcean Summary: After comparing order book depth on centralized exchanges at four time points, CoinDesk Research found that the USD depth for Bitcoin and Ethereum is now higher than during the crash and at the beginning of 2025 and 2026, indicating genuine position accumulation by market makers. Meanwhile, USD depth for altcoins has weakened continuously since early 2025, with weekly spot trading volumes still about two-thirds lower than during the crash week. For those still treating the “altcoin season” as the default path for liquidity rotation, this marks a structural turning point one year later. The order books for Bitcoin and Ethereum are deeper than before the crash, while altcoin liquidity continues to drain, and spot trading volumes remain far below the peak seen in October 2025. The order books for Bitcoin and Ethereum are deeper than they were on the day of the crash and at the beginning of 2025 and 2026, and the increase in USD terms reflects market makers deploying more capital, not just lower coin prices. Altcoin liquidity, on the other hand, has moved in the opposite direction: USD depth has steadily declined since early 2025, a trend masked by falling token prices. Weekly spot trading volume has declined by nearly two-thirds compared to the week of the crash, despite roughly doubling from the August low. One year after the largest forced liquidation event in crypto history, market "pipelines" show divergent narratives. Order book liquidity for Bitcoin and Ethereum is now higher than on the day of the crash or at the beginning of this year; smaller-cap tokens and spot trading have not followed suit. Several days after reaching a historic high of over $126,000, Bitcoin dropped to around $122,600 during early trading on October 10, 2025. Hours later, it fell below $105,000, with a significant portion of the decline occurring during thin trading hours on Friday evening in the U.S., when President Donald Trump announced a 100% tariff on Chinese imported goods. Over $19 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated in a single day. To measure the subsequent recovery, CoinDesk Research compared the market depth of major centralized exchanges at four points in time: January 1, 2025; October 10, 2025; January 1, 2026; and this week. Depth refers to the value of buy and sell orders near the current price. The deeper the order book, the larger the volume of large trades that can be absorbed without significantly moving the price. The order book for Bitcoin is now deeper than at any previous point mentioned. On October 7, there were approximately $11.7 million in orders within a 1% price range. This represents about a 75% increase compared to the crash day a year ago, and is higher than the approximately $9 million at the beginning of this year and the roughly $6.9 million at the start of 2025. This is not a price effect. Bitcoin is currently trading at about two-thirds of its pre-crash price, so the deeper order book in dollar terms reflects market makers committing more capital, not just coins becoming cheaper. Improvements are concentrated near the price—the range where market makers are most active. Further out, at a 5% distance from the price, depth is approximately $24 million, roughly returning to levels seen in January 2025. Ethereum's recovery has been stronger in some respects. Depth within a 0.5% price range has more than doubled since the crash day, reaching approximately $4.2 million. At the 1% level, depth has risen by about three-quarters to approximately $5.3 million, surpassing both January readings. "The deepening of major cryptocurrencies represents real capital, not a price effect," said CoinDesk researcher Saksham Diwan. The rebuilt order book underwent an initial test earlier this week. As the market sold off, Bitcoin’s 1% depth decreased by approximately 12% between October 7 and October 8. The tightest spread bands for Ethereum slightly widened, while orders further away from the price increased. For altcoins, the picture is exactly the opposite. In CoinDesk Research’s altcoin basket, USD depth was highest on January 1, 2025, and has been lower at every subsequent measurement point. Depth at 5% from the price has declined by about one-third since early 2025, to approximately $2 million. At the closer 1% level, it has decreased by about one-sixth. Measured by token volume, altcoin depth appears healthier: it peaked on January 1 of this year and has since declined only modestly. However, analysts note that the "recovery" in token units has been primarily driven by price declines, masking the ongoing erosion of committed capital. Spot trading has not yet resumed. According to CoinDesk Research, the average weekly spot trading volume on centralized exchanges over the four weeks ending September 27 was approximately $279 billion, nearly two-thirds lower than the $801 billion recorded during the crash week. Activity hit its lowest point in August, when weekly trading volume dropped to around $135 billion, and has since doubled. However, it remains far below levels seen before and after the crash. On October 10, 2025, crypto liquidity evaporated within hours. Where it would go next was an open question. “A year ago, we wrote that liquidity was thin and fragmented, and it was unclear where capital would rotate once the dust settled. Now we have the answer: Bitcoin and Ethereum,” said Joshua de Vos, Head of Research at CoinDesk. “Market makers have returned to major cryptocurrencies, with liquidity now exceeding pre-crash levels, while altcoin liquidity as a whole continues to decline. Beyond a select few altcoins, I expect this divergence to persist into next year, as major cryptocurrencies will continue to dominate institutional interest and trading volume.”

extraction.body: Garmin smartwatches are widely considered some of the best that money can buy, especially for serious fitness enthusiasts . In fact, Garmin practically dominates the premium smartwatch market, defined as smartwatches that cost $500 or more. If you've invested in a Garmin smartwatch (or any other brand, for that matter), it's natural to be curious how long your device will actively receive software updates and support. Generally, Garmin watches receive regular software updates until a new model is released. This typically equates to two to three years of consistent updates, especially for some of Garmin's popular product lines like the Vivoactive and the Fenix. Currently, several Garmin smartwatch models receive regular software updates, including the Forerunner (170, 570, 70, 970), Fenix 8/Fenix 8 Pro, Fenix 9/Fenix 9 Pro, Venu (4, X1), Vivoactive 6 and Instinct 3. Bug fixes and other minor updates may continue to be released for several years, regardless of the model. Garmin watches vary widely in battery life depending on the model you buy. The Lily 2 and Lily 2 Classic can last for five days in smartwatch mode on a single charge. However, some of Garmin's higher-end models, like the Fenix 8 and the Enduro 3, can last over 30 days on a single charge. The Vivofit and Vivofit Jr. can last up to one year on a single charge. With solar charging, the Instinct 3 technically has an unlimited battery life. This is one benefit of a Garmin smartwatch compared to an Apple Watch . The total lifespan of a Garmin watch may vary significantly based on how often you use it and under what conditions. For instance, a smartwatch used by a dedicated swimmer may have a slightly shorter lifespan than the same watch owned by a non-swimmer because of consistent exposure to pool chemicals or saltwater. Three to six years appears to be a typical lifespan, based on reviews and reports from forums like Reddit. Personally, I can attest to the quality of Garmin watches. I have a Vivoactive 3 that still works well, even though it's nearly a decade old. It is lacking several of Garmin's newest features, but the watch itself is still in great shape. The easiest way to ensure that you get every update is to opt in for automatic software updates. This is the default setting for most Garmin smartwatches, and you can turn it off in the Garmin Connect app settings if you prefer to install updates manually. When a new update is available, you'll receive a notification through the Garmin Connect app. You can then choose when to install the update. Alternatively, you can use the Garmin Express app on Windows and Mac computers. This app will notify you when a software or map update is available. It will also help you install updates by providing instructions tailored to your Garmin device. Additionally, Garmin publishes news about significant new software updates on its blog or through press releases, and you can also sign up for emails from Garmin to get the latest news about software and map updates sent to your inbox. sources.title: What Does Long-Term Software Support For MacBooks Actually Include? - BGR
passages: Apple devices generally get software support for years.
Similar to the iPhones, MacBooks have a long software support period and can get major software updates for seven to eight years.
A good example to show Apple's typical MacBook software support policy is the 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2019.
However, as part of the complimentary phone support, the company won't help with data recovery in case your MacBook requires a macOS reinstallation.

A good example to show Apple's typical MacBook software support policy is the 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2019. extraction.body: Apple devices generally get software support for years. For example, the company releases major iOS updates for iPhones for anywhere from five to seven years. Even after major software updates are stopped, Apple continues to provide important security patches for many more years to ensure that iPhone devices aren't left unprotected from emerging security threats. Similarly, Apple Watch models can get major OS updates for around six years, and AirPods for three years . But what about the company's MacBooks? Similar to the iPhones, MacBooks have a long software support period and can get major software updates for seven to eight years. A good example to show Apple's typical MacBook software support policy is the 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2019. This Intel-powered machine received the macOS 26 Tahoe update but didn't get the macOS 27 Golden Gate update, showing seven years of support for major updates. Similarly, the M1-powered MacBook models that were released nearly six years ago are still receiving major macOS updates. Even after Apple stops releasing new macOS feature updates for MacBook models, the company continues to release bug fixes and security patches. It typically supports two older macOS versions with these security updates for each new macOS version. This means the 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2019, which isn't getting macOS 27 Golden Gate, will continue to get security updates for around two more years in the form of updates to macOS 26 Tahoe. macOS 27 was officially rolled out on September 14, and since then, macOS 26 has already seen two notable security updates in the form of macOS version 26.7 and version 26.7.1. While these updates didn't include any new features, the 16-inch MacBook Pro (2019) got key fixes that address major security issues. Although Apple doesn't officially claim this two-year support period, it has traditionally followed this pattern. Notably, in some rare cases, Apple can even release bug fixes or security patches after these two years. For example, macOS Big Sur and macOS Catalina, which were originally introduced back in 2020 and 2019, respectively, received an update fixing the certificates for FaceTime and Messages apps in February 2026, ensuring they continue to run on older machines. Such instances aren't common but can happen. Besides all the software updates and security patches a MacBook gets, Apple offers complimentary software support for all MacBooks for the first 90 days of your device ownership. Basically, when you buy a new MacBook, you can reach out to Apple via phone to deal with any issues regarding macOS installation, launch, and reinstallation for the first 90 days, and the company will help you. There is no limit on how many times you can call Apple for this complimentary support. This can be pretty helpful to folks who are migrating to macOS from other platforms and are using Apple's operating system for the first time. However, as part of the complimentary phone support, the company won't help with data recovery in case your MacBook requires a macOS reinstallation. Although not explicitly mentioned in Apple documentation, software issues related to third-party apps are very likely not covered as well because the company has no control over them.

Even after major software updates are stopped, Apple continues to provide important security patches for many more years to ensure that iPhone devices aren't left unprotected from emerging security threats. Similarly, Apple Watch models can get major OS updates for around six years, and AirPods for three years . But what about the company's MacBooks? Similar to the iPhones, MacBooks have a long software support period and can get major software updates for seven to eight years.

A good example to show Apple's typical MacBook software support policy is the 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2019. This Intel-powered machine received the macOS 26 Tahoe update but didn't get the macOS 27 Golden Gate update, showing seven years of support for major updates. Similarly, the M1-powered MacBook models that were released nearly six years ago are still receiving major macOS updates.

Even after Apple stops releasing new macOS feature updates for MacBook models, the company continues to release bug fixes and security patches. It typically supports two older macOS versions with these security updates for each new macOS version. This means the 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2019, which isn't getting macOS 27 Golden Gate, will continue to get security updates for around two more years in the form of updates to macOS 26 Tahoe. macOS 27 was officially rolled out on September 14, and since then, macOS 26 has already seen two notable security updates in the form of macOS version 26.7 and version 26.7.1. While these updates didn't include any new features, the 16-inch MacBook Pro (2019) got key fixes that address major security issues.

Although Apple doesn't officially claim this two-year support period, it has traditionally followed this pattern. Notably, in some rare cases, Apple can even release bug fixes or security patches after these two years. For example, macOS Big Sur and macOS Catalina, which were originally introduced back in 2020 and 2019, respectively, received an update fixing the certificates for FaceTime and Messages apps in February 2026, ensuring they continue to run on older machines. Such instances aren't common but can happen.

There is no limit on how many times you can call Apple for this complimentary support. This can be pretty helpful to folks who are migrating to macOS from other platforms and are using Apple's operating system for the first time.

So I started replacing them one by one with open-source alternatives that had active communities and enough real-world credibility to survive daily use.
Its voice typing is also still better than most alternatives (whether open- or closed-source), especially if you dictate messages often.
It has a clean Material Design interface, breadcrumbs, archive support, root support for devices that need it, and network storage support through FTP, SFTP, SMB, and WebDAV.
I did not start this experiment out of ideology.
I have a Google account; I use a stock Android phone, and I have no interest in removing Google from my life entirely.
But after years of using the official apps simply because they were already there, I couldn't bear how much they expected from me in return.
I'm talking about account sign-ins, cloud habits, ecosystem nudges, and features built around what a company would prefer me to use next.
Firefox is a free, open-source web browser developed by Mozilla, focused on speed, privacy, and security for users on all major platforms.
Firefox respects the same web standards, runs uBlock Origin properly (Chrome on Android still doesn't), and lets me control DNS-over-HTTPS settings directly in the app.
The tab syncing works fine through a Mozilla account, which is optional rather than assumed.

Standing out as the best Android keyboard for privacy , HeliBoard gives me that.
The biggest win is psychological as much as technical, which is that it has no internet permission, so I do not have to think about what my keyboard could be doing.

It syncs tabs across devices, handles most sites without complaint, and benefits from years of performance work.
About Joplin: it supports a limited set of extensions also on Android.
The best of MakeUseOf, directly in your inbox.
It is one of the few Google apps that can still make a strong practical case for itself.

extraction.body: I did not start this experiment out of ideology. I have a Google account; I use a stock Android phone, and I have no interest in removing Google from my life entirely. I still want Android to feel like Android. But after years of using the official apps simply because they were already there, I couldn't bear how much they expected from me in return. I'm talking about account sign-ins, cloud habits, ecosystem nudges, and features built around what a company would prefer me to use next. So I started replacing them one by one with open-source alternatives that had active communities and enough real-world credibility to survive daily use. Some swaps faded out after a week or two because they were too awkward, too limited, or too much effort to justify. These six stayed, though. Subscription fatigue is real, and these apps are the cure. Gboard is one of the best examples of Google making an official app that is really hard to beat. It is fast to type with, quite accurate, multilingual, and excellent at glide typing. Its voice typing is also still better than most alternatives (whether open- or closed-source), especially if you dictate messages often. The problem is that a keyboard is not just another app. It sits under almost everything I type, including passwords, private messages, searches, notes, and half-finished thoughts I delete before sending. Google has done a lot to make Gboard's intelligence privacy-conscious, but I still prefer my keyboard to be boring by design. Standing out as the best Android keyboard for privacy , HeliBoard gives me that. extraction.body: I realized recently how much of my phone life quietly depends on Google. Calendar for appointments, Keep for random thoughts, Chrome for basically everything, Maps when I’m lost, and Authenticator when Google decides I need another security code. It’s convenient, sure. But I started wondering why I was handing so much of my everyday digital life to one company. I’m not trying to delete Google from my phone overnight. But I also don’t need every app on my phone reporting back to the same ecosystem. So I started replacing some of my everyday Google apps with my new favorites. I switched from Chrome to Brave after noticing how often I was opening Chrome without even thinking about it. I’d use it to check a restaurant menu, research an article, compare prices — and somehow end up with 15 tabs open. Chrome wasn’t bad; I was just tired of feeling locked into Google for every little thing. Brave felt like something I'd known for years, so switching was easy. The biggest difference I noticed was the built-in ad and tracker blocking. When I’m reading an article or shopping online, I don’t feel like the internet is following me everywhere. I no longer install a variety of extensions, which is a plus. Brave became the browser I opened automatically. For me, that’s probably the best test of a replacement. Google Keep was my go-to app. I used it for article ideas, itineraries, packing lists, or even my frustration. But NotallyX gives me something I appreciate more: the option to keep my notes local instead of making cloud syncing central to the experience. I can also lock my notes with a PIN or biometric authentication, which is useful for anything I’d rather not leave completely exposed. I also like that NotallyX isn’t limited to plain text. I can attach images or PDFs, create task lists with subtasks, set reminders, and even record quick audio notes. So when I’m working on an article and suddenly think of a headline while I’m away from my laptop, I can save it immediately. For my everyday notes , that simplicity is exactly what makes NotallyX an easy replacement. Fossify Calendar works with the calendar data already on my phone, so I can keep things like my daughter’s drawing class, my appointments, meetings, and family plans without adding another calendar service or cloud account to the mix. It also doesn’t use ads or tracking, and Fossify says it doesn’t require Internet permission or run its own cloud sync service. Here, I can customize in a million ways. For example, I can change notification sounds, vibrations, themes, calendar views, and even use home-screen widgets. I can also filter events, which is handy when my calendar starts looking like a wall of appointments. For me, that makes Fossify more than a Google Calendar clone. Google Authenticator does its job, but Aegis made me realize I was settling for a very basic 2FA app. I use authenticator codes for accounts I really don’t want to lose access to, so I like having more control over them. Aegis stores my tokens in an encrypted vault I can protect with a password or biometrics. I can also organize accounts into groups, which is surprisingly useful once the list starts filling up. The features I appreciate most are backup and export. If I switch phones, I don’t want to discover that my entire 2FA setup is trapped on the old one. Aegis lets me create encrypted backups and import or export my tokens, so moving to another phone is much less stressful. Google Maps is everyone’s first choice. Still, Organic Maps surprised me by handling the basics without keeping me tied to Google. My favorite feature is offline maps. Before a trip, I can download a map for an area and navigate even when my internet connection disappears. That’s especially useful when I’m traveling to my village or driving through areas with unreliable coverage. Organic Maps also offers turn-by-turn navigation, walking and cycling routes, saved places, and detailed points of interest. I can save places I want to visit this year and access them later. I still use Google Maps when I need live traffic or when I’m using Android Auto , but Organic Maps has become a capable offline backup. I’m not pretending I’ve completely removed Google from my life. That would be unrealistic after years of using the same apps without thinking twice. But trying these alternatives reminded me that I actually have choices. I don’t have to stick with an app simply because it’s the default. I still use Google when I need to. I just don’t need it for everything anymore. Google was starting to get on my nerves. So I ditched it entirely on my phone after trying these 4 apps. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. extraction.body: I did not start this experiment out of ideology. I have a Google account; I use a stock Android phone, and I have no interest in removing Google from my life entirely. I still want Android to feel like Android. But after years of using the official apps simply because they were already there, I couldn't bear how much they expected from me in return. I'm talking about account sign-ins, cloud habits, ecosystem nudges, and features built around what a company would prefer me to use next. So I started replacing them one by one with open-source alternatives that had active communities and enough real-world credibility to survive daily use. Some swaps faded out after a week or two because they were too awkward, too limited, or too much effort to justify. These six stayed, though. Subscription fatigue is real, and these apps are the cure. Gboard is one of the best examples of Google making an official app that is really hard to beat. It is fast to type with, quite accurate, multilingual, and excellent at glide typing. Its voice typing is also still better than most alternatives (whether open- or closed-source), especially if you dictate messages often. The problem is that a keyboard is not just another app. It sits under almost everything I type, including passwords, private messages, searches, notes, and half-finished thoughts I delete before sending. Google has done a lot to make Gboard's intelligence privacy-conscious, but I still prefer my keyboard to be boring by design. Standing out as the best Android keyboard for privacy , HeliBoard gives me that. It is based on AOSP and OpenBoard, has a clean layout, supports themes, gestures, clipboard tools, and multilingual typing, and does not try to turn the keyboard into a content hub. The biggest win is psychological as much as technical, which is that it has no internet permission, so I do not have to think about what my keyboard could be doing. The trade-off is obvious. I lose Google's best-in-class voice typing, GIF search, and some prediction magic. I am fine with that because I mostly want a keyboard that types, corrects, and stays out of the way. HeliBoard is a Android keyboard app that combines customizable themes, advanced gesture controls, clipboard management, and powerful shortcuts, enabling users to enhance typing speed, efficiency, and personalization on mobile devices Chrome on Android is a competent browser. It syncs tabs across devices, handles most sites without complaint, and benefits from years of performance work. It also ties every browsing session to a Google account by default, sends browsing data to Google's servers to power "enhanced" features, and gives you no real control over what leaves your device. Firefox respects the same web standards, runs uBlock Origin properly (Chrome on Android still doesn't), and lets me control DNS-over-HTTPS settings directly in the app. The tab syncing works fine through a Mozilla account, which is optional rather than assumed. I'd be lying if I said Chrome's cross-device integration wasn't slightly tighter, but Firefox's extension support on Android is the kind of thing I use every day, and Chrome just doesn't have it. Firefox is a free, open-source web browser developed by Mozilla, focused on speed, privacy, and security for users on all major platforms. It includes advanced features like tabbed browsing, a built-in password manager, private browsing mode, strong tracker blocking, and customization through thousands of extensions and themes. Google Photos is probably the hardest app on this list to replace. Its search is excellent, its editing tools are useful, and its automatic memories are often clever enough to make me forget how much data I am handing over. It is one of the few Google apps that can still make a strong practical case for itself. That also makes it one of the apps I most wanted to move away from. My photo library is not just a pile of images. It is receipts, documents, family pictures, location history, screenshots, travel, work, and private moments that say a lot about my life. Ente is the replacement that makes the most sense for me because it keeps the cloud backup model while changing the trust model. It is cross-platform and end-to-end encrypted, which matters when the app handles years of personal photos. For daily use, it gives me the part of Google Photos I actually need, which includes backup, organization, albums, sharing, and access from other devices. The downside is that I give up some of Google's AI-driven convenience. Search is not as uncanny, editing is not as rich, and moving a large library out of Google Photos can be annoying. Ente also has paid storage beyond its free tier. I still prefer it because my photo app should not make me wonder what else my pictures are being used to understand. Ente is a browser-based photo gallery with a companion app that is similar in function and appearance to Google Photos. It is privacy-focused, making it a good alternative to many online photo galleries. I can relate to why people love Google. I open it, type a note, pin it, color it, add a reminder, and it appears everywhere my Google account exists. For shopping lists and throwaway thoughts, it is hard to complain. However, my problem is that Keep starts to strain once notes become actual reference material. Everything lives in a grid of cards; organization depends heavily on labels and search; and exporting to a more durable workflow is not exactly pleasant. It is a sticky-note app that keeps trying to pass as a notebook. As a polished open-source note-taking app , Joplin is heavier, but in a useful way. It gives me notebooks, Markdown, attachments, tags, search, desktop apps, and sync options that are not limited to one company's ecosystem. I can use Joplin Cloud, Dropbox, OneDrive, Nextcloud, or WebDAV, and I can enable end-to-end encryption to protect my notes before they leave my device. It is not as instantly friendly as Keep. The interface is denser, setup takes more thought, and shared household notes are easier in Google's world. But for notes I want to keep, search, move, backup, and own, Joplin is the better tool. Joplin is a cross-platform, privacy-focused note-taking and task-management app. It supports rich features like Markdown notes, notebooks and tags, end-to-end encryption, a web clipper, self-hosted sync (via WebDAV/Nextcloud/Dropbox) or managed cloud sync with Joplin Cloud. It works offline, allows importing from Evernote, supports plugins and themes, and gives full control over your data. Google Calendar is excellent if your life already runs through Gmail, Meet, Tasks, and shared Google accounts. It pulls events from emails, handles invites well, and makes multiple calendars easy to manage. I would not tell someone with a work-heavy Google setup to abandon it casually. On my personal phone, though, I do not need my calendar to be another Google command center. I want dates, reminders, recurring events, widgets, and a clean monthly view. So I replaced Google Calendar with Fossify Calendar , which does that without making the app feel tied to a wider productivity machine. It opens quickly, looks clean, supports local calendars, reminders, recurring events, widgets, and color coding, and gives me enough customization for scheduling. It also pairs nicely with CalDAV sync if I want a more open setup across devices. A clean, open-source calendar app that keeps your events local and free from tracking. Files by Google is good at what Google wants it to be good at. It finds junk, suggests cleanup actions, highlights downloads, and makes file management less scary for casual users. I understand why it exists. I also find it too opinionated. I do not always want cleanup cards, category views, and suggestions. Sometimes I want to browse actual folders, move files properly, inspect storage, work with archives, or connect to a server without feeling as if the app is protecting me from the file system. Serving as a criminally underrated open-source Android file manager, Material Files is much closer to what I want from a file manager. It has a clean Material Design interface, breadcrumbs, archive support, root support for devices that need it, and network storage support through FTP, SFTP, SMB, and WebDAV. Everything lives in a grid of cards; organization depends heavily on labels and search; and exporting to a more durable workflow is not exactly pleasant. It is a sticky-note app that keeps trying to pass as a notebook.

As a polished open-source note-taking app , Joplin is heavier, but in a useful way. It gives me notebooks, Markdown, attachments, tags, search, desktop apps, and sync options that are not limited to one company's ecosystem. I can use Joplin Cloud, Dropbox, OneDrive, Nextcloud, or WebDAV, and I can enable end-to-end encryption to protect my notes before they leave my device.

It is not as instantly friendly as Keep. The interface is denser, setup takes more thought, and shared household notes are easier in Google's world. But for notes I want to keep, search, move, backup, and own, Joplin is the better tool.

Joplin is a cross-platform, privacy-focused note-taking and task-management app. It supports rich features like Markdown notes, notebooks and tags, end-to-end encryption, a web clipper, self-hosted sync (via WebDAV/Nextcloud/Dropbox) or managed cloud sync with Joplin Cloud. It works offline, allows importing from Evernote, supports plugins and themes, and gives full control over your data.

Google Calendar is excellent if your life already runs through Gmail, Meet, Tasks, and shared Google accounts. It pulls events from emails, handles invites well, and makes multiple calendars easy to manage. I would not tell someone with a work-heavy Google setup to abandon it casually.

On my personal phone, though, I do not need my calendar to be another Google command center. I want dates, reminders, recurring events, widgets, and a clean monthly view. So I replaced Google Calendar with Fossify Calendar , which does that without making the app feel tied to a wider productivity machine. It opens quickly, looks clean, supports local calendars, reminders, recurring events, widgets, and color coding, and gives me enough customization for scheduling. It also pairs nicely with CalDAV sync if I want a more open setup across devices.
A clean, open-source calendar app that keeps your events local and free from tracking.

Files by Google is good at what Google wants it to be good at. It finds junk, suggests cleanup actions, highlights downloads, and makes file management less scary for casual users. I understand why it exists.

I also find it too opinionated. I do not always want cleanup cards, category views, and suggestions. Sometimes I want to browse actual folders, move files properly, inspect storage, work with archives, or connect to a server without feeling as if the app is protecting me from the file system.

Serving as a criminally underrated open-source Android file manager, Material Files is much closer to what I want from a file manager. It has a clean Material Design interface, breadcrumbs, archive support, root support for devices that need it, and network storage support through FTP, SFTP, SMB, and WebDAV.

These swaps do not ask you to rebuild your entire relationship with your phone. Each one addresses a specific frustration I had with the official version, and each one delivers on its core function without the overhead I was trying to avoid. Start with the one that bothers you most. The open-source Android ecosystem is in a stronger state than it's ever been, and the apps in it have stopped asking you to make apologies for using them.

extraction.body: I realized recently how much of my phone life quietly depends on Google. Calendar for appointments, Keep for random thoughts, Chrome for basically everything, Maps when I’m lost, and Authenticator when Google decides I need another security code. It’s convenient, sure. But I started wondering why I was handing so much of my everyday digital life to one company. I’m not trying to delete Google from my phone overnight. But I also don’t need every app on my phone reporting back to the same ecosystem. So I started replacing some of my everyday Google apps with my new favorites. I switched from Chrome to Brave after noticing how often I was opening Chrome without even thinking about it. I’d use it to check a restaurant menu, research an article, compare prices — and somehow end up with 15 tabs open. Chrome wasn’t bad; I was just tired of feeling locked into Google for every little thing. Brave felt like something I'd known for years, so switching was easy. The biggest difference I noticed was the built-in ad and tracker blocking. When I’m reading an article or shopping online, I don’t feel like the internet is following me everywhere. I no longer install a variety of extensions, which is a plus. Brave became the browser I opened automatically. For me, that’s probably the best test of a replacement. Google Keep was my go-to app. I used it for article ideas, itineraries, packing lists, or even my frustration. But NotallyX gives me something I appreciate more: the option to keep my notes local instead of making cloud syncing central to the experience. I can also lock my notes with a PIN or biometric authentication, which is useful for anything I’d rather not leave completely exposed. I also like that NotallyX isn’t limited to plain text. I can attach images or PDFs, create task lists with subtasks, set reminders, and even record quick audio notes. So when I’m working on an article and suddenly think of a headline while I’m away from my laptop, I can save it immediately. For my everyday notes , that simplicity is exactly what makes NotallyX an easy replacement. Fossify Calendar works with the calendar data already on my phone, so I can keep things like my daughter’s drawing class, my appointments, meetings, and family plans without adding another calendar service or cloud account to the mix. It also doesn’t use ads or tracking, and Fossify says it doesn’t require Internet permission or run its own cloud sync service. Here, I can customize in a million ways. For example, I can change notification sounds, vibrations, themes, calendar views, and even use home-screen widgets. I can also filter events, which is handy when my calendar starts looking like a wall of appointments. For me, that makes Fossify more than a Google Calendar clone. Google Authenticator does its job, but Aegis made me realize I was settling for a very basic 2FA app. I use authenticator codes for accounts I really don’t want to lose access to, so I like having more control over them. Aegis stores my tokens in an encrypted vault I can protect with a password or biometrics. I can also organize accounts into groups, which is surprisingly useful once the list starts filling up. The features I appreciate most are backup and export. If I switch phones, I don’t want to discover that my entire 2FA setup is trapped on the old one. Aegis lets me create encrypted backups and import or export my tokens, so moving to another phone is much less stressful. Google Maps is everyone’s first choice. Still, Organic Maps surprised me by handling the basics without keeping me tied to Google. My favorite feature is offline maps. Before a trip, I can download a map for an area and navigate even when my internet connection disappears. That’s especially useful when I’m traveling to my village or driving through areas with unreliable coverage. Organic Maps also offers turn-by-turn navigation, walking and cycling routes, saved places, and detailed points of interest. I can save places I want to visit this year and access them later. I still use Google Maps when I need live traffic or when I’m using Android Auto , but Organic Maps has become a capable offline backup. I’m not pretending I’ve completely removed Google from my life. That would be unrealistic after years of using the same apps without thinking twice. But trying these alternatives reminded me that I actually have choices. I don’t have to stick with an app simply because it’s the default. I still use Google when I need to. I just don’t need it for everything anymore. Google was starting to get on my nerves. So I ditched it entirely on my phone after trying these 4 apps. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

sources.title: CrowdStrike vs. ServiceNow: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? - Yahoo Finance
passages: CrowdStrike focuses on stopping data breaches through its unified Falcon platform, while ServiceNow streamlines complex business workflows using artificial intelligence.
Both companies dominate their respective niches, but their financial profiles and risk factors differ significantly as we head into late 2026.
CrowdStrike's massive stock price run-up so far in 2026 reflects the explosive nature of all things AI-related.

Growth-minded investors looking to capitalize on the growing urgency and complexity of cybersecurity in an increasingly AI-driven world may be drawn to CrowdStrike stock despite its premium multiples and unprofitability.
Indeed, its partnership with Amazon is a vote of confidence in its cybersecurity product.
Software leaders are redefining the modern workplace through security and automation.
But choosing between CrowdStrike (NASDAQ:CRWD) and ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) requires weighing hypergrowth potential against proven profitability and platform stability.
It primarily reaches enterprise and government customers through a network of resellers and managed service providers.
ServiceNow offers a broader software suite than CrowdStrike, which may appeal to investors looking for more stability.

Ironically, one of its current challenges may be the same sentiment that has juiced CrowdStrike's business: a fundamental wariness to introduce artificial intelligence technology across an organization's operations.
That said, the company is consistently profitable and the stock trades at a steep discount to CrowdStrike's.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Sarah Sidlow has positions in Microsoft and Nvidia.
The Motley Fool recommends the following options: long January 2028 $260 calls on Accenture Plc and short January 2028 $280 calls on Accenture Plc.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.2x, while the current ratio of 1.8x suggests ample liquidity for short-term liabilities.
Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 68% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $4.8 billion, representing a 21.7% increase compared with the prior fiscal year.
Despite this growth, the company reported a net loss of approximately $162.5 million, which led to a negative net margin of 3.4%.
Net margin measures how much of every dollar in revenue actually remains as profit after all expenses.
The company relies on a massive partner ecosystem including Accenture (NYSE:ACN), Infosys (NYSE:INFY), and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).
In its latest annual report, the company noted that nearly 200 million employees interact with its portal each month.
CrowdStrike faces ongoing reputational damage and potential customer churn following a major content configuration update incident in July 2024.
It operates in a crowded market against legacy antivirus vendors and faces active securities litigation stemming from that system crash.
The company also relies heavily on Amazon for its cloud infrastructure and must manage the risks of complying with global data privacy laws.
ServiceNow competes with massive enterprise software rivals like Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and new entrants focused solely on artificial intelligence.
It also faces risks related to managing complex customer contracts and potential service disruptions to its third-party cloud infrastructure.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
*Stock Advisor returns as of October 7, 2026.
ServiceNow appears more conservatively valued in this comparison, trading at lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio multiples relative to earnings estimates and sales over the past 12 months.

Since its launch back in 2009, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) has gained an absolutely incredible 134,900,000%. For good reason, it has acquired a reputation as a potential millionaire maker.

But that was then. The days of Bitcoin's stratospheric annual returns may be coming to an end. As institutional investors pile into Bitcoin , it is increasingly behaving like a high-beta tech stock. Thus, it's going to be a lot harder to turn $1,000 into $1 million.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The math behind any potential millionaire-maker coin is relatively simple, at least when the contemplated investment is small. The only way to turn $1,000 into $1 million is if the coin has 1,000x upside potential.
At one time, Bitcoin had this type of upside potential. It's how the cryptocurrency went from a $1 price tag to a $1,000 value, and from $100 to $100,000.

But is that still the case? From a current price of $85,000, Bitcoin would need to skyrocket to $85 million. That's preposterous, and well beyond the price target of even the most bullish Bitcoin investor. Take Michael Saylor of Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR), for example. He thinks Bitcoin is headed to $21 million in 21 years .

Just think of the math involved if Bitcoin were to hit a price of $85 million. Right now, Bitcoin has a market cap of $1.7 trillion. So 1,000x upside implies a future market cap measured in the quadrillions, not the trillions. That simply does not make any kind of sense.

Or, think of it another way. Bitcoin at a price of $85 million would be worth nearly 1,000 times the current value of Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX). Right now, SpaceX has a market cap of $2.2 trillion.

That being said, it is possible to think of a few alternative paths to millionaire status. For example, investors could dabble in Bitcoin derivatives (such as perpetual futures) or Bitcoin prediction market contracts.

In both cases, investors can take on tremendous leverage, setting up the opportunity for massive gains (as well as crushing losses). On Kalshi, for example, retail investors can take on 6.8x leverage when trading Bitcoin perpetual futures.

So, in this hypothetical scenario, an investor might be able to transform $1,000 into $10,000 using leverage. Then, that money could be plowed into the spot crypto market. In this scenario, Bitcoin would only need 100x upside potential. That's still asking a lot of Bitcoin, but at least the numbers start to make at least a little more sense.
Long story short, the most likely path to millionaire status is by spotting the potential of a cryptocurrency investment early, long before anyone else thinks it's valuable.
That was the case with Bitcoin in the early days, when nobody could imagine it even reaching $10, $100, or $1,000. Now it's worth $85,000.

The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Bitcoin wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

Now, it's worth noting Stock Advisor's total average return is 950% — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 215% for the S&P 500. Don't miss the latest top 10 list, available with Stock Advisor , and join an investing community built by individual investors for individual investors.

BitMine Immersion Technologies chairman Tom Lee said Ethereum should top $5,000 by year-end, in Singapore on Friday. That was half the $10,000 year-end figure Lee called "conservative" when he also said Ethereum would trade "much higher" than that level within 12 months. His cycle target came down too, to "25,000 or 50,000 per token" from an illustrative $62,000 nine days earlier. Ethereum (ETH) held above $2,400 on Saturday after BitMine Immersion Technologies (BMNR) chairman Tom Lee said the token should top $5,000 by year-end, half the level he called a "conservative target" more than a week ago. Speaking at Token 2049 in Singapore on Friday, Lee, who is also co-founder and head of research at Fundstrat, tied the call to Bitcoin (BTC). If Bitcoin climbs to $100,000, he said, Ethereum should trade around $7,500. That was a step down from what he called FLOP Labs' CEO Arthur Hayes' $10,000 year-end prediction for Ethereum "conservative ," last month. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. To support his point, Lee said, "Think Arthur's conservative in the sense that you know in the past cycles Ethereum has gone up 50 times to 200 times." On Friday, the cycle number was lower too. Ethereum "could easily be 25,000 or 50,000 per token," he said. Lee called the token "massively undervalued," pointing to years of sideways trading. The longer the base, he said, the bigger the breakout. The market, however, shows something different. Bitcoin's (BTC) dominance has risen to about 57.5%, while Ethereum's sat near 10.5%. Ethereum's price traded relatively flat over the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Ethereum remained in the 'bearish' zone, with chatter at 'normal' levels over the last day. Lee argued this cycle will outrun past ones because of who was buying. Earlier rallies ran on retail money, first through initial coin offerings and later through non-fungible tokens (NFTs). This time, he said, institutions were building real products on blockchains. Investors "aren't bullish enough," he said, and should expect "some monster moves in crypto prices." Lee pointed to Ethereum's developer base and its record without downtime. He also warned large banks that ignore crypto. He said firms that fail to build a crypto strategy risk becoming "the National Cash Register (NCRs) and the Microwave Communications, Inc. (MCIs) of this era," referring to two companies he said missed major technology shifts. BMNR stock closed little changed on Friday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BMNR remained in the 'bearish' zone, with chatter at 'normal' levels over the past day. This impressive performance has led traders to wonder if we are entering an altcoin season.
Leading the charge is NEAR Protocol (CRYPTO:NEAR), which has surged 121%, far outpacing Bitcoin's 6.4% gain over the same period.
The Altcoin Season Index formalizes this concept, declaring altcoin season only when 75% of the 50 largest coins outperform Bitcoin over a 90-day timeframe.
Still, three reasons suggest the possibility of a longer rally.
First, Bitcoin also dropped 2% over the past week, suggesting the altcoin declines occurred during a broader market dip rather than a rotation back into Bitcoin.
Two, two of the eight coins are still climbing.
Lastly, a one-week period is a brief timeframe for assessing market trends.
Furthermore, the impressive 30-day gains took place without any clear news driving them.
The other seven coins making waves are Sui (CRYPTO:SUI), Aave (CRYPTO:AAVE), Avalanche (CRYPTO:AVAX), Uniswap (CRYPTO:UNI), Litecoin (CRYPTO:LTC), Hedera (CRYPTO:HBAR), and Cardano (CRYPTO:ADA).
Even Cardano, at the bottom of the list, boasts a respectable 20% gain—more than three times Bitcoin's increase.

Altcoins are any cryptocurrencies aside from Bitcoin, and "altcoin season" describes a phase when traders shift funds out of Bitcoin and into smaller coins, leading to substantial gains for most altcoins.
Conversely, a "Bitcoin season" occurs when Bitcoin outperforms the majority of the market.

For example, Cardano would need to increase roughly 12 times its current value to reclaim its prior record, making a 20% monthly gain seem minimal in that context. A negative MVRV indicates that typical buyers are at a loss.
For XRP, the MVRV sits at about -11.8%, while Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Chainlink are slightly above zero, reflecting a more favorable outlook for their holders.
This performance has affected holder returns, with XRP and Dogecoin seeing larger losses while Bitcoin remains relatively stable.
Currently, XRP is priced at $1.51 and Bitcoin at $84,388.
With these figures in mind, which coin is likely to rally next?
Its holders are nearing break-even, meaning few hold large profits to cash out.
Furthermore, the strong interest in spot ETFs suggests ongoing institutional buying support.
Although XRP’s holder losses indicate a potential setup for recovery, much of that action has already occurred with its recent climb.
Bitcoin is poised for its next move primarily through institutional buying rather than relying just on holder losses.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs attracted about $1.7 billion in investments on September 21 and 22, signaling strong investor interest.
Earlier this year, Santiment noted that XRP’s 365-day MVRV had plummeted to around -47% in July, marking a historic low.
Since then, XRP has bounced back roughly 32% to $1.51, bringing its MVRV up to about -12%.
This recovery has allowed many holders who were deeply in the red to either sell or benefit from the upward price movement.
Meanwhile, XRP still has significant room to grow, trading 36% below its January 6, 2026 peak of $2.36.
Despite attempts to break above $1.60 on September 22 and 23, XRP closed below this level both times.
Additionally, XRP funds saw inflows of only $10 million to $19 million a week in September, suggesting slower momentum than Bitcoin.

XRP holders have endured a painful stretch while Bitcoin investors sit near break-even, and now both coins are flashing signals that suggest a major move is coming for one of them.

However, if Bitcoin ETF investments fall and outflows increase, it could lose its current momentum, regardless of its MVRV readings.

This suggests an interesting dynamic between the two coins, as XRP and Bitcoin seem to be on opposite ends of the spectrum in terms of holder profit.
Currently, XRP is priced at $1.51 and Bitcoin at $84,388. With these figures in mind, which coin is likely to rally next?

Santiment’s figures come from the 365-day MVRV (Market Value to Realized Value), which gauges a coin’s current price against the average price paid by holders over the past year. A negative MVRV indicates that typical buyers are at a loss. For XRP, the MVRV sits at about -11.8%, while Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Chainlink are slightly above zero, reflecting a more favorable outlook for their holders.

XRP’s price dropped about 17% in 2026 and roughly 48% over the past year, while Bitcoin has dropped only about 3% this year. This performance has affected holder returns, with XRP and Dogecoin seeing larger losses while Bitcoin remains relatively stable.

This recovery has allowed many holders who were deeply in the red to either sell or benefit from the upward price movement.

Comparatively, Bitcoin has also recovered, moving from an MVRV of about -26.6% in March to near break-even. However, the MVRV metric only accounts for coins that are actively moved, missing buying activity that remains on exchanges.

Bitcoin is poised for its next move primarily through institutional buying rather than relying just on holder losses. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs attracted about $1.7 billion in investments on September 21 and 22, signaling strong investor interest.

Although XRP’s holder losses indicate a potential setup for recovery, much of that action has already occurred with its recent climb.

If XRP closes above $1.60—just about a 6% uplift from its current price—especially with increasing fund buying, it could surge. However, if Bitcoin ETF investments fall and outflows increase, it could lose its current momentum, regardless of its MVRV readings.

Six of the eight outperforming altcoins have already reversed lower this week, with Uniswap erasing nearly half its monthly gains in seven days.
The Altcoin Season Index sits at 51, well below the 75 threshold required to declare a season, and no true altcoin season has occurred in 379 days.

Over the last 30 days, eight altcoins have seen returns at least three times greater than Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC). This impressive performance has led traders to wonder if we are entering an altcoin season. Leading the charge is NEAR Protocol (CRYPTO:NEAR), which has surged 121%, far outpacing Bitcoin's 6.4% gain over the same period.

The other seven coins making waves are Sui (CRYPTO:SUI), Aave (CRYPTO:AAVE), Avalanche (CRYPTO:AVAX), Uniswap (CRYPTO:UNI), Litecoin (CRYPTO:LTC), Hedera (CRYPTO:HBAR), and Cardano (CRYPTO:ADA). Even Cardano, at the bottom of the list, boasts a respectable 20% gain—more than three times Bitcoin's increase.

Traders often see such a leaderboard as potential evidence of an altcoin season. However, six of these eight coins have declined over the past week, and the Altcoin Season Index still hasn't reached its critical levels. So, the question remains: Are we truly starting an altcoin season, or is this just a short-term bounce?

Altcoins are any cryptocurrencies aside from Bitcoin, and "altcoin season" describes a phase when traders shift funds out of Bitcoin and into smaller coins, leading to substantial gains for most altcoins. Conversely, a "Bitcoin season" occurs when Bitcoin outperforms the majority of the market.

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

That is exactly what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps answer. It covers what your retirement could actually cost, which income sources are worth using, and the withdrawal math that decides whether the money lasts. It is free today from Fisher Investments. Read More Here ›

The Altcoin Season Index formalizes this concept, declaring altcoin season only when 75% of the 50 largest coins outperform Bitcoin over a 90-day timeframe. As of October 10, 2026, the index is at 51, indicating that we are "not in Altcoin Season." Remarkably, it has been 379 days since the last altcoin season and 39 days since the last Bitcoin season.

CoinMarketCap's version of the index showed 61 on October 1, which also falls short of the 75 threshold. Both indexes intentionally measure a 90-day period to prevent a single strong month from prematurely indicating a season.
Only NEAR (up 13%) and Cardano (up 3%) have maintained an upward trend over the past week. Meanwhile, the other six coins have experienced declines.

Uniswap has taken the biggest hit, with its UNI token still up 25% over 30 days despite a 19% drop in the past week, erasing nearly half of its earlier gains. Similarly, Hedera has slipped by 9%, while Litecoin decreased by 8%.

This quick unwind points to a temporary bounce, since the rotation reversed within the same month it began. In a lasting trend, altcoins typically continue to outperform Bitcoin week after week, but many of these coins stopped that trend before the month ended.

Still, three reasons suggest the possibility of a longer rally. First, Bitcoin also dropped 2% over the past week, suggesting the altcoin declines occurred during a broader market dip rather than a rotation back into Bitcoin. Two, two of the eight coins are still climbing. Lastly, a one-week period is a brief timeframe for assessing market trends. Furthermore, the impressive 30-day gains took place without any clear news driving them.

A bigger concern for these coins is how far they fell before this recent recovery. Each of the eight coins is trading substantially below its all-time high. For instance, Avalanche is down 93% from its peak, while Cardano is down 92%, and Litecoin, Hedera, and Uniswap have each fallen between 83% and 85%.
Sui is down 79%, and NEAR and Aave are both down 74%. In contrast, Bitcoin is down 34% from its peak.

A coin that has lost more than 90% can still rise substantially and linger far below previous price levels, because the gain starts from a much lower base. For example, Cardano would need to increase roughly 12 times its current value to reclaim its prior record, making a 20% monthly gain seem minimal in that context. A leaderboard ranking by percentage gains tends to favor coins that faced the biggest declines, as they rebound from lower starting points.

The current 30-day outlook suggests the start of an altcoin season, but the evidence leans toward a bounce. Six of the eight coins have already turned negative over the past week, and the Altcoin Season Index stands at 51, far below the 75 threshold needed for a season call. A genuine altcoin season requires sustained outperformance across the 50 largest coins over several months, and a handful of coins showing short-term gains does not provide enough support for such a declaration.

For holders of these coins, the index serves as a vital indicator. A reading of 75 or higher would contradict the bounce scenario and signal the first altcoin season in 379 days. Conversely, if the index stays below that level and more of these eight coins decline over the next week, it may suggest the recent surge was more of a fleeting bounce than the start of a sustained altcoin season.

This impressive performance has led traders to wonder if we are entering an altcoin season.
Leading the charge is NEAR Protocol (CRYPTO:NEAR), which has surged 121%, far outpacing Bitcoin's 6.4% gain over the same period.
The Altcoin Season Index formalizes this concept, declaring altcoin season only when 75% of the 50 largest coins outperform Bitcoin over a 90-day timeframe.
Still, three reasons suggest the possibility of a longer rally.
First, Bitcoin also dropped 2% over the past week, suggesting the altcoin declines occurred during a broader market dip rather than a rotation back into Bitcoin.
Two, two of the eight coins are still climbing.
Lastly, a one-week period is a brief timeframe for assessing market trends.
Furthermore, the impressive 30-day gains took place without any clear news driving them.
The other seven coins making waves are Sui (CRYPTO:SUI), Aave (CRYPTO:AAVE), Avalanche (CRYPTO:AVAX), Uniswap (CRYPTO:UNI), Litecoin (CRYPTO:LTC), Hedera (CRYPTO:HBAR), and Cardano (CRYPTO:ADA).
Even Cardano, at the bottom of the list, boasts a respectable 20% gain—more than three times Bitcoin's increase.

Altcoins are any cryptocurrencies aside from Bitcoin, and "altcoin season" describes a phase when traders shift funds out of Bitcoin and into smaller coins, leading to substantial gains for most altcoins.
Conversely, a "Bitcoin season" occurs when Bitcoin outperforms the majority of the market.
A reading of 75 or higher would contradict the bounce scenario and signal the first altcoin season in 379 days.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Similarly, Hedera has slipped by 9%, while Litecoin decreased by 8%.
This quick unwind points to a temporary bounce, since the rotation reversed within the same month it began.
In a lasting trend, altcoins typically continue to outperform Bitcoin week after week, but many of these coins stopped that trend before the month ended.
Sui is down 79%, and NEAR and Aave are both down 74%.
In contrast, Bitcoin is down 34% from its peak.
